{ "item": { "id": "3cc1aa67-f674-447d-8dda-ac55a42c26eb", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Connectors", "short_description": "What a connector is in Godzilla: a pre-built integration to a source or destination system, with its own auth and catalog of built-in types.", "body": "

Connectors

A connector is a pre-built integration to an external system that a Pipeline reads from or writes to. Connectors handle authentication, batching, and retry behavior for a specific system so pipeline authors don't have to.

Connector direction

  • Source — emits events into a pipeline (e.g. a change-data-capture stream from Postgres).
  • Destination — receives events from a pipeline (e.g. writing rows into Snowflake).
  • Bidirectional — a small set of connectors, like the generic Webhook connector, can act as either.

Built-in connector catalog

ConnectorDirectionAuth
PostgresSourceConnection string + replication slot
Amazon S3Source / DestinationIAM role or access key
SnowflakeDestinationKey-pair auth
KafkaSource / DestinationSASL/SSL
WebhookSource / DestinationSigned request or bearer token
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Rotating connector credentials|body_html=

Rotating a connector's credentials pauses any pipeline using it for the duration of the rotation. Plan credential rotations outside peak processing windows.

}}

Connector health

Each connector reports a health status independent of any single pipeline: healthy, degraded, or down. A connector shared across multiple pipelines only needs to be fixed once — every pipeline referencing it recovers automatically.

See also

Connectors are configured per pipeline in the Connecting a data source guide, and referenced directly in the Connectors endpoint of the API reference.

", "version_token": "6ef91311-b169-42cc-9373-c908e2ab9e18", "created_at": "2026-08-22T00:49:50.810Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-22T00:50:01.027Z", "placement_id": "e008cc85-c171-4744-8db3-24b6237d037d", "folder_id": "6dd1d477-874c-4c27-bab8-e07308ae4f25", "file_name": "concepts-connectors" } }

{ "item": { "id": "93eecc21-ad7e-43ae-a9d5-a0301ad65f1d", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Connecting a data source", "short_description": "Choose the right connector type and authentication method for a new data source.", "body": "

Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
An existing event streamKafka
A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Next steps

With a source connected, follow Building your first pipeline to wire it into a full pipeline.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/2df76640-838b-4256-956e-d8a19a602241}}|prev_label=Building your first pipeline|next_href={{cms:item/b8a1e50e-1ef9-425d-b3d1-4e1b3cb6368f}}|next_label=Transforming events in flight}}", "version_token": "694b83fa-cd2f-4107-a8dc-745e0eb0bf73", "created_at": "2026-08-22T00:34:13.294Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-22T00:34:26.065Z", "placement_id": "65da7cd3-3805-439a-ab83-5342997746aa", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "connecting-a-data-source" } }

Connectors endpoint {{ds:component/chip|label=v2|variant=primary}}

Manage connectors — the source and destination integrations pipelines read from and write to.

POST /v2/connectors

POST /v2/connectors/{id}/rotate — pauses every pipeline referencing this connector for the duration of the rotation, then resumes them automatically.

A connector referenced by multiple pipelines is rotated once, for all of them. Check a connector's pipeline_count field before rotating during a busy window.

}}

{ "item": { "id": "34f15418-1e32-455b-8b41-2f0bc73f5b68", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Backfill historical data", "short_description": "Techniques and configurations for loading historical data ranges through Godzilla pipelines.", "body": "

Backfill historical data

Backfilling lets you stream historical data from your storage or database into downstream targets — bootstrapping new destinations, backpopulating historical records, or replaying data after schema changes.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you begin|body_html=

Ensure your source connector supports range queries or timestamp filtering. See Connecting a data source for connector details.

}}

1. Define a time-bounded source connector

Configure your source connector with start and end timestamps (or watermarks) to define the historical boundary. This prevents the backfill job from processing live events prematurely.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=backfill-source.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"postgres\", \"direction\": \"source\", \"config\": { \"connection_string\": \"postgres://user:secret@db.example.com:5432/production\", \"query\": \"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01T00:00:00Z' AND created_at < '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'\", \"timestamp_column\": \"created_at\" } }}}

2. Set batch size and concurrency controls

Historical backfills often involve large data volumes. Adjust your pipeline's batch size and concurrency limit to avoid exhausting memory or triggering rate limits on your destination system.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-backfill.json|language=json|code={ \"name\": \"orders-backfill-2025\", \"source_connector_id\": \"conn_pg_orders_backfill\", \"destination_connector_id\": \"conn_snowflake_dw\", \"settings\": { \"batch_size\": 5000, \"concurrency\": 4, \"max_retries\": 5 } }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Destination throughput|body_html=

Monitor destination write latency while the backfill runs. If destination response times spike, reduce pipeline concurrency.

}}

3. Run and monitor the backfill

Start the pipeline using the Pipelines endpoint. You can inspect event throughput and error rates via Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=run-backfill.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines/orders-backfill-2025/start \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\"}}

4. Transitioning to real-time streaming

Once the backfill reaches the cutoff timestamp, switch the pipeline configuration or activate your real-time streaming pipeline. Godzilla ensures idempotent writes when keys are configured, preventing duplicate entries during handoff.

Next steps

Learn how to handle failed records during backfills in Error handling & recovery, or query processed records using the Events endpoint.

{ "item": { "id": "4ab406d1-6af0-4c0c-8097-b123e2f76e73", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Scheduling & triggers", "short_description": "Run a pipeline on a cron schedule or trigger it directly from incoming events.", "body": "

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ \"schedule\": \"0 */4 * * *\" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Error handling & recovery.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/c484e924-5ec5-4c95-81ad-c8c31b702a7f}}|prev_label=Error handling & recovery|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}", "version_token": "48663fb1-36e6-41b3-90ba-083793406827", "created_at": "2026-08-22T00:46:57.463Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-22T00:47:41.321Z", "placement_id": "8ed279da-c9eb-46e0-bd2f-4f15df9f1c76", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "scheduling-and-triggers" } }

{ "item": { "id": "c69c120c-89e9-4c48-bac8-ff67efa372b6", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Building your first pipeline", "short_description": "Create a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that connects them, end to end.", "body": "

Building your first pipeline

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

}}

1. Create a source connector

We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"type":"postgres","direction":"source","config":{"connection_string":"postgres://..."}}'}}

2. Create a destination connector

We'll write to Snowflake.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"type":"snowflake","direction":"destination","config":{"account":"..."}}'}}

3. Create the pipeline

Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v3/pipelines \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \ -d '{"name":"ingest-orders","source_connector_id":"conn_pg_orders","destination_connector_id":"conn_snowflake_dw"}'}}

The pipeline starts in draft state. Activate it once you're ready to start processing events.

Next steps

Now that events are flowing, read Error handling & recovery to see what happens when a write fails, or Monitoring & alerts to watch it run.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/dedb99ab-0330-4db5-84cf-bd4661ea3545}}|prev_label=Guides|next_href={{cms:item/59a8507a-08b2-49f3-9f37-775cfbebc5d3}}|next_label=Transforming events in flight}}", "version_token": "f533e14b-bd82-4e4f-8352-a9ed70626d5d", "created_at": "2026-08-22T00:51:47.610Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-22T00:51:59.681Z", "placement_id": "546623a3-eb81-48dc-8562-eb2751ef9082", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "building-your-first-pipeline" } }

{ "item": { "id": "7f879624-4206-4511-82fa-99ec3f5b86cc", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Concepts", "short_description": "The core building blocks and key definitions of Godzilla: pipelines, connectors, events, schemas, and terminology.", "body": "{{ds:component/hero|title=Concepts|subtitle=The core building blocks every Godzilla pipeline is made of.|cta_html=Start with Pipelines}}

Godzilla is built from core concepts that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

{{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/0881cc13-706b-45dc-b215-08b706dc8fdb}}|tag=Concept|title=Pipelines|description=Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/3cc1aa67-f674-447d-8dda-ac55a42c26eb}}|tag=Concept|title=Connectors|description=Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/aaba4e33-be69-4693-8066-1c2f622b674b}}|tag=Concept|title=Events|description=The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.}} {{ds:component/card|href={{cms:item/88ecedb3-543b-4dcf-b985-6fb94e4eaa95}}|tag=Concept|title=Schemas|description=Declarative contracts that define and validate the structure of event payloads flowing through pipelines.}}

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, validates their schemas, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that single loop.

Definitions

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Schema
A declarative contract specifying the structure, types, and validation rules for event payloads.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Error handling & recovery.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Rate limits.
Quota
Usage allowances assigned to a workspace based on its plan tier, covering request throughput and monthly event volume. See Quotas & billing.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.

Pipelines

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

  • Source — the connector that emits events into the pipeline (a database, a queue, an upload, a webhook).
  • Transforms — an ordered list of steps that reshape, filter, or enrich events as they pass through. Transforms are optional; a pipeline with none is a pass-through copy.
  • Destination — the connector that events are written to once transforms complete.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Pipelines are declarative|body_html=

You describe the desired source, transforms, and destination; Godzilla schedules and retries the runs. You never manage worker processes directly.

}}

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • draft — configured but not yet processing events.
  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Pipeline configuration is versioned. Publishing a new version does not affect events already in flight on the previous version — in-flight runs finish on the version they started on. This matters most when a pipeline definition is part of a larger migration; see the Migration guide for an example of retiring an old pipeline version safely.

Next steps

Ready to build one? Start with the Building your first pipeline guide, or jump straight to the Pipelines endpoint in the API reference.

args.body:
Connectors

A connector is a pre-built integration to an external system that a Pipeline reads from or writes to. Connectors handle authentication, batching, and retry behavior for a specific system so pipeline authors don't have to.

Connector direction

  • Source — emits events into a pipeline (e.g. a change-data-capture stream from Postgres).
  • Destination — receives events from a pipeline (e.g. writing rows into Snowflake).
  • Bidirectional — a small set of connectors, like the generic Webhook connector, can act as either.

Built-in connector catalog

ConnectorDirectionIncremental readsAuth
PostgresSourceYesConnection string + replication slot
Amazon S3Source / DestinationYesIAM role or access key
SnowflakeDestinationNoKey-pair auth
KafkaSource / DestinationYesSASL/SSL
WebhookSource / DestinationNoSigned request or bearer token
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Rotating connector credentials|body_html=

Rotating a connector's credentials pauses any pipeline using it for the duration of the rotation. Plan credential rotations outside peak processing windows.

}}

Connector health

Each connector reports a health status independent of any single pipeline: healthy, degraded, or down. A connector shared across multiple pipelines only needs to be fixed once — every pipeline referencing it recovers automatically.

See also

Connectors are configured per pipeline in the Connecting a data source guide, and referenced directly in the Connectors endpoint of the API reference.
